title: After Congress, expanded nutrition program bill’s next test is funding
summary: Education Secretary Sonny Angara highlights the need for adequate funding for the proposed law to be effective, as budgets fall short of the required amounts for comprehensive feeding programs

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – Efforts to strengthen the country’s feeding program to address malnutrition and learning gaps moved forward in Congress with the national children’s nutrition bill.
On Monday, November 23, the Senate ratified the reconciled version of the bill, which seeks universal feeding for kindergarten to Grade 3 public school students, according to Senator Bam Aquino.
The final version of the proposed law must still be sent to Malacañang. Once signed by President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., it would amend the Masustansyang Pagkain para sa Batang Pilipino Act.

The measure, a Marcos priority bill, would establish the national nutrition program, which introduces the “life-stage approach.” It essentially seeks to replace the fragmented implementation of feeding programs and align nutrition interventions from the first 1,000 days up to 11 years old, as well as for pregnant adolescent students.

“It’s an ambitious program…. The coverage is one hot meal per day for at least 200 days,” Pasig City Representative Roman Romulo, the chairman of the House committee on basic education and culture, told Rappler.
Romulo also noted that under the bill, there should be an increase in meal funding, which should be directly spent on food costs and not cover maintenance and operating expenses.
The bill also mandates sourcing products from local farmers and fisherfolk for the hot meals.

Citing the findings of the Second Congressional Commission on Education (EDCOM 2), Romulo said the government must address stunting early on as it would be “close to impossible” to reverse its lasting consequences later in life.
EDCOM 2 also earlier raised concern that the stunting rate among children under five years old reached 25.3% in 2025, a 1.7% increase from 2023 and the first uptick since 2015.
But while the bill’s approval in Congress shows progress, Education Secretary Sonny Angara is still keeping his feet on the ground.

“Higit sa lahat, ang mas importante sa batas ay pondohan ‘yong batas. ‘Yong batas, salita lang. ‘Pag walang pondo ‘yong batas, wala tayong pagkain na ipapakain sa bata,” he said on the sidelines of the 2nd Southeast Asia Regional School Meals Coalition Summit in Mandaluyong City on Monday.
(More than anything else, what’s more important is funding for the proposed law. The law would just be mere words. If the law is unfunded, we wouldn’t be able to provide meals for the children.)

Romulo told Rappler that during technical working group meetings on the bill, some members of the mayors’ league warned that funding constraints could hamper the implementation of proposed changes to the feeding program. They also said municipalities would need capacity-building support.
He said the bill therefore ensures that fourth- and fifth-class municipalities will be prioritized for funding augmentation from the national government.
But even if the bill is signed into law this year, the target universal coverage of the Department of Education (DepEd) — kindergarten to Grade 3 — will not be immediately reached in 2027.
Aquino’s manifestation during Monday’s plenary session already pointed to attempts at looking for additional funding to expand the universal coverage only up to Grade 2 for next year.

blocks.text: Pending actual figures from the Senate’s plenary debates, the school-based feeding program’s 2027 budget remains at P11 billion, roughly the same figure in the National Expenditure Program (NEP) and the House version of the budget bill.
The proposed P11-billion funding is significantly lower than the P25.7 billion in the 2026 national budget.
Previously, Angara asked senators for an additional P16.82 billion to at least implement a 180-day feeding cycle for kindergarten and Grade 1.
To run a program for 200 days for kindergarten to Grade 2, lawmakers would have to inject at least P28 billion more. This coverage would benefit 6.88 million learners, according to DepEd projections.

The budget for the supplemental feeding program for children under five years old, handled by the Department of Social Welfare and Development, is a different matter. That too has a lower budget under the 2027 NEP.

Given the reality of limited funding, EDCOM 2 Executive Director Karol Mark Yee said the bill allows for the “progressive and phased implementation” of the national nutrition program. But the National Nutrition Council will already lead the creation of a five-year roadmap for the execution and financing plan.

“We need to make sure that the five-year roadmap is actually very concrete and very targeted…. What we really need to make sure of is that the agencies are working together,” Yee told Rappler in a recent interview.
Part of the process is harmonizing government instruments and assessments so that there will only be one reference in identifying nutritionally-at-risk and undernourished children.
Yee said the reform includes the establishment of a “unified health record,” mandating the government to track the nutritional status of children.
Reacting to the developments, the World Food Programme said it is coordinating with the DepEd in improving the country’s feeding program, adding that local implementation may be a “real challenge.”

“The law is important. It sets the foundation for some of these changes, but we need to see it implemented…. LGUs (local government units) have such an important role to play in a relatively decentralized government system. And so, getting key LGUs on board is critical,” Regis Chapman, WFP representative and country director in the Philippines, said in a chance interview.
